newsitem.title: UK: UK govt--Benefit fraud scheme saves 100 mln pounds.
newsitem.headline: UK govt--Benefit fraud scheme saves 100 mln pounds.

text.p: A British government scheme to clamp down on fraudulent welfare payment claims has saved more than 100 million pounds in its first year, Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley said on Wednesday.

"The Spotlight Campaign" against benefit cheats, launched last March, has encouraged thousands of people to put their claims in order or to sign off benefits altogether, Lilley said. As a result, 101 million pounds ($162.2 million) has been saved.
"And for the first time, there are signs that anti-fraud measures are deterring potential cheats from ripping off the benefit system," Lilley said.

He said the scheme, which operates in certain key areas across the country, has helped cut Britain's unemployment figures which have been tumbling consistently. In January, the jobless rate of 6.5 percent was the lowest since 1990.
"Claimant unemployment has been falling steadily since 1993, as the economy has grown. But in Spotlight areas the number of claimants has been dropping more steeply than in the rest of Britain."
The scheme involved sending 150,000 forms to benefit claimants asking them if their circumstances had changed. Of the 75 percent so far returned, around one in five reported changes.

"The Spotlight campaign coincided with sharp reductions in claimant unemployment in the areas targeted, and with a dramatic increase in the amount of benefit savings from all anti-fraud activities, from 886 million pounds in 1994/95 to some 1.4 billion in 1995/96," Lilley said.

As part of his November budget, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke announced a wider "spend-to-save" scheme to crack down on benefit fraud. The scheme would save nearly seven billion pounds over three years, Clarke said.

But the Treasury Select Committee said in January that it doubted that figure would be met. "We are concerned that there is a risk that modest increases in expenditure on 'spend to save' will not yield the forecast large increases in receipts over the planning period," it said in a report.
Lilley said the public response to another part of the campaign -- the National Benefit Fraud Hotline -- showed people's attitude to benefit cheats.

"My message to those who persist in cheating is clear: Be warned. You are not only up against the Benefits Agency's fraud investigators. You also face the overwhelming disapproval of the vast majority of honest people throughout Britain."
Last November, the government said the hotline, which encourages people to call in with information about possible welfare cheats, had received 100,000 calls in three months.
Earlier on Wednesday, Employment Minister Eric Forth launched a campaign to encourage the unemployed to take up voluntary work.

"The aim of the Jobseeker's Allowance (JSA) is to get people back into employment," he said. "I believe jobseekers can benefit in their job search from the valuable skills and experience gained by working with charities, voluntary organisation and public bodies.
The JSA, which replaced old-style unemployment benefit late last year, makes extra demands on claimants to prove they are actively seeking work.

The Office for National Statistics has warned that a backlog of unprocessed claims, caused by the switchover, has kept the total claimant count -- which makes up the official jobless figures -- artificially low.
